meta.what: Cost, schedule, team and total cost of ownership for software projects · v2.2.0 · open source (MIT)
meta.subtitle: Describe a software project, or let the app count its code, and get the development cost, timeline, team size and total cost of ownership from the COCOMO II model, with a PDF you can forward. No technical background needed.
authoritative_sources: Boehm et al., Software Cost Estimation with COCOMO II (2000)
The app's methodology page (last page of every PDF report)
meta.disclaimer: Estimates are decision support, not quotes. The ±30% range reflects typical COCOMO II accuracy for uncalibrated projects; confirm scope and rates with your team before committing budget. This page is non-controlled.

chapters.headline: The gut number nobody can defend.
chapters.intro: Someone asks what an application would cost to build, or rebuild, or keep running. The answer is usually a round number from memory, a spreadsheet that drifts, or a generic calculator that has never heard of a codebase with R, Python and SQL in it.

items.title: Spreadsheets drift
items.text: Every copy has a different rate, a different premium for rush work, and no record of why.

items.title: A single figure hides the risk
items.text: Software estimates are wide by nature. A number without a range invites a budget that is wrong on day one.

items.title: Deadlines are negotiated blind
items.text: Nobody can say what a shorter timeline costs, or whether the team you have can meet it at all.

items.title: The reasoning is lost
items.text: By the time the number reaches a decision, the assumptions behind it are gone.

chapters.headline: A number, its range, and every assumption behind it.
chapters.intro: The estimator runs the published COCOMO II model over your line counts and a handful of plain-language choices, then shows the result as a decision, not a dashboard.

items.label: ESTIMATE RANGE
items.text: the typical accuracy of this class of model, shown on every screen and in the PDF
items.source: Boehm et al., Software Cost Estimation with COCOMO II (2000)

items.label: RUSH PREMIUM
items.text: what compressing the schedule below its natural length can add, growing smoothly instead of in steps
items.source: Model: ratio^1.25 anchored to COCOMO II's SCED driver, capped at 2.0 (README, Methodology)

items.label: TESTS
items.text: lock the engine, the formatting, the share link and the one cost decomposition every chart reads

chapters.headline: From lines of code to a budget, one factor at a time.
chapters.intro: Every step is visible in the app's waterfall chart, and the steps always sum exactly to the headline figure.

items.title: Count and weight the code
items.text: Languages are detected and weighted for productivity. Documentation and configuration files are shown but never counted toward the cost.

items.title: Effort from size and complexity
items.text: Effort grows faster than size: a high-complexity project of the same length costs more than a simple one.

items.title: Experience, reuse, tooling
items.text: Plain-language choices such as 'Excellent tooling' or 'Very high reliability' map to the published multipliers.

items.title: Your team and your deadline
items.text: A schedule cap shorter than the natural schedule adds a rush premium. A plan that needs more people than your team cap is flagged as not feasible.

items.title: Person-months to dollars
items.text: Effort is priced at one fully loaded cost per developer-year. Doubling the rate doubles the estimate.

items.title: Keeping it running
items.text: Maintenance is a share of the build cost each year, escalating 5%, shown nominal and discounted so the total cost of ownership is honest.

chapters.headline: It will not pretend to know more than it does.
chapters.intro: The estimator is built so that a forwarded number never disagrees with itself and never looks more precise than it is.

summary: Every view reads the same steps.

items.text: The engine is published COCOMO II with documented calibration; 297 tests lock it.

items.title: Is shown everywhere

cta.headline: Get your first estimate in two minutes.
cta.intro: The guide walks you from the worked example to a shared PDF, with a checkpoint at each step.

welcome.title: Open the app and run the example
welcome.intro: The estimator runs in the browser; nothing to install. The first screen shows a worked example you can run in one click, so you see a complete estimate before you type anything.

items.title: Open the app
items.text: Use the link at the top of this page, or the Live App link in the project README. It works on a phone, but the charts are easier to read on a laptop.

items.title: Choose Run this example
items.text: The example is 10,000 lines of R at medium complexity with a proficient team. The result appears on the right with every section filled.

items.title: Find the Help menu
items.text: Top right: this guide, a short how-to, the parameter reference and the release notes. The sun/moon button switches light and dark mode.

blocks.alt: First-run screen with the worked example and the three ways to bring in code
blocks.caption: The first screen: a worked example and the three ways to bring in code.

welcome.checkpoint: I can open the app, run the example, and see the headline cost with its range.

first-estimate.title: Describe your own project
first-estimate.intro: A rough guess is fine. The point of the first pass is to see how the number moves when you change something, not to get it right the first time.

items.title: Keep Manual selected under 'Where is the code?'
items.text: Type roughly how many lines of code the project has, split by language. If you only know a total, put it all in one language.

items.title: Set the three inputs that matter most
items.text: Complexity (when in doubt, Medium), Team experience (1 novice to 5 expert) and Cost per developer-year (the fully loaded yearly cost of one developer, salary plus benefits and overhead).

items.title: Choose Run estimate
items.text: The button at the bottom of the inputs counts the code and shows the result. On a phone, the inputs drawer closes so the result is what you see.

items.title: Move a slider
items.text: Drag the Schedule cap to the left. The cost rises, the status line explains why, and you did not need to run anything again.

blocks.title: Only line counts and uploads need Run estimate.
blocks.text: Every other input recalculates the estimate the moment it changes. The note under the headline figure reminds you of this.

blocks.html: Changed your mind? Reset returns every parameter to its default, and a toast offers Undo for fifteen seconds.

first-estimate.checkpoint: I have run an estimate for my own line counts and watched it change when I moved the schedule cap.

headline.title: The headline block
headline.intro: Everything a budget conversation needs is in the first block: the figure, how sure the model is, whether the plan is feasible, and what the number rests on.

aside.title: Budget on the range, not the point
aside.text: The low and high ends are equally plausible. Treat the figure as the middle of a band, and read the status line before you quote it.

items.label: The figure
items.text: Estimated development cost, rounded to the nearest $1,000 so it never looks more precise than it is.

items.label: The range
items.text: ±30% drawn on a scale that starts at $0, so you can see how wide the uncertainty is.

items.label: The status line
items.text: Within plan, Compressed schedule (with the premium), or Not feasible with this team cap.

items.label: The scope line
items.text: Billable lines, complexity, team experience, rate and source: exactly what the number is based on.

items.title: Schedule tile
items.text: The schedule against your cap, with the natural schedule the model would have chosen. A warning word appears when it is compressed or over the cap.

items.title: Team tile
items.text: People in full-time equivalents against your team cap. 2.4 FTE means roughly two full-time developers plus one part-time.

items.title: Ownership tile
items.text: Total cost of ownership in today's dollars: the build cost plus the maintenance years you chose. With maintenance off, the tile shows effort in person-months instead.

blocks.alt: The Estimate page scrolled: ranked drivers, languages, sensitivity and ownership sections open
blocks.caption: Below the headline block, each section answers one question.

headline.checkpoint: I can find the figure, its range, the status line and the scope line, and I know which tile shows total cost of ownership.

sections.title: The sections, one question each
sections.intro: The first two sections are open. Click any heading to open the rest. Every chart card can be expanded to full screen, and a summary strip keeps the cost and a PDF button in reach while you scroll.

items.title: How is the cost built?
items.text: A waterfall from base effort through every factor to the final figure. The bars are labelled and sum exactly to the estimate.

items.title: What if the deadline moves?
items.text: Cost at every schedule cap from 3 to 60 months. The diamond is your cap. Shaded caps are shorter than the natural schedule and carry a rush premium; hollow points would need more people than your team cap allows.

items.title: Which choices matter most?
items.text: The same factors as the waterfall, ranked by dollars. Bars to the left save money; bars to the right add cost.

items.title: What is the code made of?
items.text: Lines by language. Grey bars are documentation and configuration, which are never billed.

items.title: How sensitive is the estimate?
items.text: Cost across team experience and complexity, with everything else held at your values. The diamond is your estimate.

items.title: What does it cost to keep running?
items.text: Build cost, maintenance over the years you chose (nominal and in today's dollars), the total cost of ownership, and what it would be at other maintenance rates.

items.title: Assumptions and data
items.text: Every input and result in a table, plus a plain-text report you can paste anywhere.

blocks.html: The waterfall, the ranked drivers, the text report, the CSV and the PDF all read the same cost steps. If two views ever disagreed, that would be a bug; it is tested.

sections.checkpoint: I know which section to open to see what a shorter deadline costs, and which one shows how the cost is built.

inputs.title: Tuning the inputs
inputs.intro: Each input has a question-mark button with a plain-language explanation. These are the ones that move the number most.

items.title: Complexity
items.text: Low: one or two screens and simple logic. Medium: several interconnected features. High: complex architecture, AI parts, real-time data. Effort grows exponentially with size at higher complexity.

items.title: Team experience
items.text: 1 to 5. Four is the baseline (proficient). More experience lowers the estimate.

items.title: Code reuse
items.text: How much existing code, packages or templates the team can lean on. More reuse, lower estimate.

items.title: Tooling and process
items.text: From 'Excellent: IDE, version control, CI/CD, tests, review' to 'Poor: no version control'. Better tooling, lower estimate.

items.title: Cost per developer-year
items.text: The fully loaded annual cost of one developer. If you only know base salary, add roughly 25 to 40%. Doubling it doubles the estimate.

items.title: Team cap
items.text: The most people on the project at once, up to 8. Six or more adds a 10% coordination premium. A smaller team means a longer schedule.

items.title: Schedule cap
items.text: The longest the project may take. Tighter than the natural schedule adds a rush premium, up to double. If the cap would need more people than your team cap, the plan is flagged as not feasible.

blocks.html: Expand Advanced COCOMO drivers for five published cost drivers, each a named level: required reliability, product complexity, required reusability, team continuity and domain experience. Nominal means no effect; the badge next to the heading shows their combined multiplier.
Leave these at nominal unless you know the project well. They are the difference between a quick estimate and a considered one, not between a wrong and a right one.

items.title: Annual maintenance rate
items.text: Yearly upkeep as a share of the build cost. 15 to 20% is typical; 25 to 30% for applications with frequent change requests or regulatory updates.

items.title: Maintenance years
items.text: How many years to include in the total cost of ownership. Three to five is a typical planning horizon; 0 shows the build cost only.

inputs.checkpoint: I know which inputs move the number most, and where to find the explanation for each one.

code-sources.title: Bringing in real code
code-sources.intro: When you do not know the line counts, let the app count them. Languages are detected automatically, and documentation or configuration files are shown but never billed.

items.title: Zip the project folder
items.text: Leave out data files, build output and virtual environments so the archive stays under 50 MB.

items.title: Choose ZIP and pick the file
items.text: The archive is extracted in an isolated temporary folder on the server, counted, and discarded.

items.title: Run estimate
items.text: The progress shows elapsed time and the file being counted. The scope line will show how many documentation lines were excluded.

blocks.html: Only available when the app runs on your own computer (for example from RStudio with shiny::runApp("cost-estimator-app")). Choose Folder, enter or browse to the repository path, and run.
On the hosted version the Folder option is hidden; use ZIP instead.
If the archive contains no source code, the app says so and offers the worked example instead of showing an empty chart.

code-sources.checkpoint: I know how to get an estimate from a repository without counting lines by hand.

scenarios.title: What-if scenarios
scenarios.intro: A budget conversation rarely ends with one number. Pin up to three versions of an estimate and compare them on the same scales.

items.title: Save as scenario
items.text: Under the headline block. The current estimate, including its language mix, advanced drivers and maintenance settings, is pinned to the Scenarios page.

items.title: Change something and save again
items.text: A shorter deadline, a smaller team, a more experienced one. Up to three scenarios.

items.title: Open Scenarios
items.text: Each scenario shows its cost, range, schedule, team and status, and an Inputs panel you can edit in place; the comparison updates as you type. One developer-year cost is shared so the dollars stay comparable.

items.title: Read the comparison
items.text: Aligned bars for cost (with its range), schedule and team, and a side-by-side table with the cost difference against Scenario 1.

blocks.alt: Scenarios page with two saved scenarios and a free third slot
blocks.caption: Two scenarios: the same project at a 9-month cap and at a 24-month cap.

scenarios.checkpoint: I have saved two scenarios and can see the cost difference between them.

share.title: Share and export
share.intro: Every way out of the app carries the same numbers, rounded the same way.

items.title: Download PDF report
items.text: A five-page document: cover with the figure, range and status; the waterfall and ranked drivers; the deadline curve and ownership over time; every assumption; how the cost is built; methodology. Takes a few seconds; the progress shows elapsed time.

items.title: Copy link
items.text: The address bar always holds a link that reopens this exact estimate. Repository scans are shared as their line counts.

items.title: CSV and JSON
items.text: The language table, the cost steps and the results for spreadsheets or other tools.

meaning.title: What the numbers mean
meaning.intro: The estimator is deliberately conservative about what it claims. Knowing its limits makes the number more useful, not less.

items.title: The range is the estimate
items.text: ±30% reflects the typical accuracy of COCOMO II for projects that have not been calibrated against their own history. Budget on the range.

items.title: Rush work costs more
items.text: Compressing the schedule below its natural length adds a premium that grows smoothly with the compression, up to double the cost.

items.title: People do not scale linearly
items.text: Six or more people add coordination overhead, and the model never uses more than eight.

items.title: Documentation is free
items.text: Only code that must be designed, written and tested drives cost. Docs and config files are listed for transparency but excluded.

items.title: Figures are rounded on purpose
items.text: To the nearest $1,000 above $100,000, so a wide estimate never reads as dollar-accurate. The engine itself is exact.

items.title: Not feasible means not feasible
items.text: When a deadline would need more people than your cap, the app says so instead of pretending the plan works.

meaning.checkpoint: I understand that the figure is the middle of a range and that the app flags plans it cannot stand behind.

faq.title: Questions people ask
faq.intro: Short answers to the questions that come up in the first week.

items.title: Why did the cost jump when I shortened the schedule?
items.text: Compressed timelines need more parallel work, senior talent and overtime. The premium grows with the amount of compression, up to double.

items.title: Why is the team size 2.4 FTE?
items.text: It is an average staffing level over the project: roughly two full-time developers plus one part-time.

items.title: Which cost per developer-year should I enter?
items.text: The fully loaded annual cost: salary plus benefits and overhead. If you only know base salary, add roughly 25 to 40%.

items.title: Can I trust a single number?
items.text: Use the range for budgeting, read the status line, and check the methodology page of the PDF for exactly how the figure is produced.

items.title: Does the app keep my code?
items.text: Uploads are extracted in a temporary folder, counted and deleted. Only the line counts per language are kept for the estimate, and only for your session.

items.title: Where does the model come from?
items.text: COCOMO II.2000 (Boehm et al.), with one documented calibration for modern frameworks. Constants and formulas are listed on the methodology page and in the README.

plan.title: Choosing a plan
plan.intro: You rarely know every input. The planner under the headline turns what you do know into exact plans, each one a real run of the model you can apply with one click.

aside.title: Every card is an engine call
aside.text: The model prices every team size against every deadline in a few milliseconds, so the advice is computed, not guessed. The text explains numbers it was handed.

items.title: Tell it what you know
items.text: People available (1 to 8), a deadline in months, a budget in dollars. All optional; fill in one, two or none.

items.title: Read the advice
items.text: A short paragraph leads with your facts: the fastest realistic delivery with your team, what one more person changes, whether the deadline can be met, whether the budget fits.

items.title: Pick a card
items.text: Cheapest, fastest practical, with your team, for your deadline, within your budget. Each shows cost, months, FTE and the caps that produce it. Apply sets those caps in the sidebar; Save pins it as a scenario.

items.title: Read the staffing curve
items.text: Months to deliver for one to eight people, with the cost on each point. The dotted line is the natural schedule with no rush; the shaded zone is where coordination overhead starts.

blocks.title: Nothing gets faster than 75% of the natural schedule.
blocks.text: That is the limit COCOMO II treats as practical (Boehm's 'impossible region'). Plans below it are drawn on the curve but never recommended, and a deadline below it is reported as not achievable with the nearest date instead.

blocks.html: When no plan fits the budget, the planner says how much of the scope would (in lines) and what one level better code reuse or tooling would save, each priced.

plan.checkpoint: I have entered my team size, read the advice, and applied a plan to the headline.
